summary_html: Cases arising on **federal lands/facilities** or involving **Indian children** invoke federal/tribal jurisdictional rules (VICAA for federal facilities; **ICWA** for Indian children and tribal preference/jurisdiction).
authority_html:
- **VICAA (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — federal-facility reporting mandates  
- **ICWA (25 U.S.C. §§ 1901–1963)** — tribal jurisdiction, placement preferences, notice to tribes

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: "Domicile" in ICWA is a uniform question of federal law, and children domiciled on a reservation fall within exclusive tribal jurisdiction that parents cannot defeat by giving birth or placing the child off-reservation.
key_cases.relevance: Establishes that ICWA's jurisdictional terms are federal and uniform, the premise Alaska courts build on when allocating authority between the superior court and Alaska Native tribal courts.
key_cases.quote: In enacting the ICWA Congress confirmed that, in child custody proceedings involving Indian children domiciled on the reservation, tribal jurisdiction was exclusive as to the States.

key_cases.case_name: State v. Native Village of Tanana
key_cases.holding: Federally recognized Alaska Native tribes may exercise inherent sovereign jurisdiction to initiate ICWA child custody proceedings without a § 1918 reassumption petition, and judgments from those proceedings may be entitled to full faith and credit by the State.
key_cases.relevance: Is the controlling Alaska authority on when a tribal forum, rather than the superior court, may open a child-protection case.
key_cases.quote: federally recognized Alaska Native tribes are not necessarily precluded from exercising inherent sovereign jurisdiction to initiate "child custody proceedings" as ICWA defines that term

key_cases.holding: Adopting the federal tribal-exhaustion doctrine, the court held that a father who failed to appeal a Minto Tribal Court termination of his parental rights through tribal appellate remedies could not collaterally attack that judgment in state court, and his suit was dismissed.
key_cases.relevance: Establishes that once a tribal court properly exercises jurisdiction, tribal remedies must be exhausted before any state-court challenge.
key_cases.quote: We therefore conclude his suit in Alaska state court must be dismissed.

key_cases.case_name: Native Village of Tununak v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: Overruling its prior application of Adoption Rule 11's preponderance standard, the court held that good cause to deviate from ICWA's adoptive placement preferences must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, and vacated and remanded for application of that standard.
key_cases.relevance: Demonstrates that ICWA supplies a federal standard of proof that displaces a conflicting Alaska court rule.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that ICWA implicitly mandates that good cause to deviate from ICWA's adoptive placement preferences be proved by clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.holding: Alaska Native tribes possess inherent, non-territorial sovereign authority to adjudicate child custody disputes between their own members in tribal court, so the superior court erred in refusing to give the Northway Tribal Court judgment effect; the case was remanded to decide whether that judgment should be recognized under comity.
key_cases.relevance: Is the foundational Alaska holding that tribal adjudicatory authority over children does not depend on Indian country, the premise on which Tanana and every later Alaska tribal-jurisdiction case rests.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that Native tribes do possess the inherent sovereign power to adjudicate child custody disputes between tribal members in their own courts

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court rejected every constitutional challenge to ICWA: Congress had Article I power to enact it, its placement and remedial-effort commands do not unconstitutionally commandeer state legislatures, courts or executive officers, and the equal-protection and nondelegation claims failed for want of standing.
key_cases.relevance: Settles that ICWA validly binds Alaska's superior courts and OCS, removing the constitutional cloud the Fifth Circuit had cast over 25 U.S.C. section 1912(d).
key_cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners’ challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

mandatory_reporters: Practitioners of the healing arts — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(1)

School teachers and school administrative staff of public and private schools, including athletic coaches — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(2); an unpaid volunteer athletic coach is not required to report unless the coach volunteers more than four hours a week for four consecutive weeks or more than 20 hours a week in a one-month period, has received the training required under Alaska Stat. § 47.17.022, and has signed a form acknowledging the duty to report — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(j)
Peace officers and officers of the Department of Corrections — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(3)
Administrative officers of institutions — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(4)
Paid employees of domestic violence and sexual assault programs and of crisis intervention and prevention programs — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(6)
Paid employees of an organization that provides counseling or treatment to people seeking to control their use of drugs or alcohol — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(7)
Members of a child fatality review team or of the multidisciplinary child protection team — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(8)
Volunteers who interact with children in a public or private school for more than four hours a week — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(9)
Juvenile probation officers and juvenile probation office staff, and staff of juvenile detention and juvenile treatment facilities — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(10)
reporting_details: Alaska is not a universal-reporting state: only the occupational categories listed in Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a) are required to report, and they must report immediately — defined as no later than 24 hours (Alaska Stat. § 47.17.290(7)) — to the nearest office of the Department of Family and Community Services, the department in which the Office of Children's Services sits (Alaska Stat. § 47.17.290(6)); if the harm appears to result from a suspected sex offense they must also report immediately to the nearest law enforcement agency. A reporter who cannot reasonably contact the nearest office of the department when immediate action is necessary for the child's well-being must instead report to a peace officer (Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(c)). Any other person may report but is not required to (Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(b)). OCS takes reports at 1-800-478-4444 or 907-269-6510, 24 hours a day, every day, and takes a written report by email at ReportChildAbuse@alaska.gov or by fax at 907-269-3939.
